left.label: Convex mirror
left.rule: Always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image. Focal length is taken positive (new Cartesian). Image lies between pole and focus on the same side as the object.
left.example: Vehicle side mirror — gives a wide field of view so every object appears smaller and farther.

right.label: Concave mirror
right.rule: Image character depends on object position: beyond C → real, inverted, diminished; between F and C → real, inverted, enlarged; inside F → virtual, erect, enlarged.
right.example: Shaving mirror (object inside F) and torch reflector (source at F).

left.label: EMF (ε)
left.rule: Energy per unit charge the source can deliver when NO current flows. Measured by a potentiometer (null method). Depends only on the cell chemistry.
left.example: A fresh 1.5 V cell with open circuit reads 1.5 V across terminals — that is its EMF.

right.label: Terminal voltage (V)
right.rule: Voltage across the cell WHILE current flows: V = ε − Ir on discharge, V = ε + Ir on charging. Measured by a voltmeter. Drops as load increases.
right.example: A car battery (ε = 12 V, r ≈ 0.05 Ω) delivering 100 A shows V = 12 − 5 = 7 V at the terminals while cranking.

left.label: SN1
left.rule: Two-step, carbocation intermediate. First-order kinetics: rate = k[RX]. Favoured by 3° substrates, polar protic solvents, and weak nucleophiles. Gives racemisation at chiral centres.
left.example: Hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide in aqueous ethanol — 3° carbocation is stable, so SN1 dominates.

right.label: SN2
right.rule: One-step, concerted backside attack. Second-order kinetics: rate = k[RX][Nu−]. Favoured by 1° substrates, polar aprotic solvents, and strong nucleophiles. Gives Walden inversion of configuration.
right.example: Reaction of methyl bromide with OH− in DMF/acetone — unhindered substrate, strong nucleophile, clean inversion.

left.label: Enthalpy (ΔH)
left.rule: Heat absorbed/released at constant pressure. Sign tells you if bonds were net made (exothermic, ΔH < 0) or broken (endothermic, ΔH > 0). Units kJ mol⁻¹.
left.example: Combustion of methane: ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹ — strongly exothermic because product bonds (C=O, O−H) are stronger than reactant bonds.

right.label: Entropy (ΔS)
right.rule: Change in the number of accessible microstates (disorder). ΔS > 0 when gases are produced, solids dissolve, or a system spreads out. Units J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ — note the unit mismatch with ΔH.
right.example: Melting of ice at 0 °C: ΔS > 0 (liquid water has more positional disorder than crystalline ice), ΔH > 0, and ΔG = 0 at equilibrium.

left.label: Interference
left.rule: Superposition of waves from TWO (or few) coherent sources. Fringes are equally spaced with β = λD/d, and all bright fringes have the same intensity. Requires a constant phase relationship — ordinary bulbs cannot interfere.
left.example: Young's double-slit with λ = 500 nm, d = 1 mm, D = 1 m gives β = 0.5 mm — the 7th bright fringe sits 3.5 mm from the centre, just as bright as the central one.

right.label: Diffraction
right.rule: Bending of a wave at an aperture or edge — effectively superposition from infinite secondary wavelets of ONE slit. Central maximum has width 2λD/a (twice the side-fringe width) and is far brighter; intensity of successive maxima falls off rapidly.
right.example: Single slit, a = 0.1 mm, λ = 600 nm, D = 2 m → central max width = 2·λD/a = 24 mm. First minimum at sin θ = λ/a, not λ/d.

left.label: Photoelectric effect
left.rule: A photon is ABSORBED by a bound electron and the electron is ejected if hν ≥ φ₀. Max KE = hν − φ₀ depends on FREQUENCY, not intensity; stopping potential rises linearly with ν (slope h/e). Photocurrent ∝ intensity.
left.example: Metal with φ₀ = 2 eV illuminated by λ = 400 nm (hν ≈ 3.1 eV): Kmax = 1.1 eV, V₀ = 1.1 V; doubling the bulb's intensity doubles the current but leaves V₀ unchanged.

right.label: Compton effect
right.rule: A photon SCATTERS off a (nearly) free electron — photon survives but with longer wavelength. Shift Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ) depends only on scattering angle, not on λ or the material. Compton wavelength h/m_ec ≈ 2.43 pm.
right.example: X-ray of λ = 0.5 Å scatters at 90°: Δλ = 0.0243 Å, giving λ' = 0.5243 Å. No threshold — any photon scatters; at θ = 0 there is no shift.

left.label: Self-inductance (L)
left.rule: Flux linkage of a coil with its OWN current: Nφ = Li, so induced emf = −L·di/dt. For a long solenoid L = μ₀N²A/ℓ. Energy stored = ½Li². Resists changes in its own current.
left.example: 50 mH coil with current rising from 3 A to 5 A in 0.2 s → induced emf = 0.05·(2/0.2) = 0.5 V; energy jumps from 0.225 J to 0.625 J.

right.label: Mutual inductance (M)
right.rule: Flux linkage of coil 2 due to the current in coil 1: N₂φ₂ = Mi₁, induced emf in coil 2 = −M·di₁/dt. For coaxial solenoids M = μ₀N₁N₂A/ℓ, and M = k√(L₁L₂) with k ≤ 1. Couples TWO circuits — basis of the transformer.
right.example: Two coils with M = 0.2 H; primary current falls from 4 A to 0 in 0.1 s → emf induced in the secondary = 0.2·(4/0.1) = 8 V.

left.label: Ionic character
left.rule: Dominates when the cation is LARGE/low-charge and the anion is SMALL/low-charge, so polarisation is weak. Favoured by large electronegativity gap; gives high-melting solids that dissolve in water and conduct when molten. Lattice energy scales as |q⁺q⁻|/(r⁺ + r⁻).
left.example: NaCl vs NaI: Na⁺ is the same, but Cl⁻ is smaller and less polarisable, so NaCl is more ionic (m.p. 801 °C) than NaI (m.p. 661 °C).

right.label: Covalent character (Fajan)
right.rule: Rises when the cation is SMALL/highly-charged and the anion is LARGE/polarisable. Fajan's rules: more covalent → lower m.p., solubility in non-polar solvents, deeper colour. Polarising power ∝ charge/radius².
right.example: AlCl₃ (Al³⁺ is small, high-charge) is covalent and sublimes at 180 °C and dissolves in benzene; compare with ionic NaCl. Similarly AgI is far more covalent than AgF.

left.label: Galvanic (voltaic) cell
left.rule: Converts chemical energy to electrical energy via a SPONTANEOUS redox reaction. E°cell > 0 and ΔG° = −nFE°cell < 0. Anode is NEGATIVE, cathode is POSITIVE. Nernst equation gives E under non-standard conditions.
left.example: Daniell cell: Zn | Zn²⁺ ‖ Cu²⁺ | Cu with E°cell = 1.10 V. For n = 2, ΔG° = −2·96500·1.10 ≈ −212 kJ/mol; the cell discharges until equilibrium (log K = nE°/0.0591).

right.label: Electrolytic cell
right.rule: Uses external electrical energy to drive a NON-SPONTANEOUS reaction (E°cell < 0). Anode is POSITIVE, cathode is NEGATIVE (opposite to galvanic). Faraday's laws: moles deposited = It/(nF). Basis of electroplating and metal extraction.
right.example: Electrolysis of molten NaCl produces Na at the cathode and Cl₂ at the anode; 1 F (96500 C) deposits 23 g Na. Cu refining, Hall–Héroult Al process are other KCET-relevant examples.

left.label: Lanthanide contraction
left.rule: Steady decrease in atomic/ionic radii across the 4f series (La → Lu) because 4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly. Consequences: Zr ≈ Hf radii, similar chemistry of 4d and 5d pairs, and higher densities of 5d metals.
left.example: r(Zr) ≈ r(Hf) ≈ 159 pm — that is why separating Zr from Hf is very hard. Also explains why Ln³⁺ radii fall from La³⁺ (103 pm) to Lu³⁺ (86 pm).

right.label: Actinide contraction
right.rule: Analogous contraction across the 5f series (Ac → Lr) but LARGER per-step shrinkage because 5f electrons shield even less effectively than 4f. Actinides also show more variable oxidation states (up to +7 in Np, Pu) and are all radioactive, unlike the mostly +3 lanthanides.
right.example: Common oxidation state of Ln is +3; U shows +3, +4, +5, +6, and Np reaches +7. Actinide contraction is the reason later actinides are hard to isolate and characterise.

left.label: Independent events
left.rule: Occurrence of one does NOT alter the probability of the other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A). Two events with positive probabilities CANNOT be both independent and mutually exclusive.
left.example: Rolling two dice — 'die 1 shows 6' and 'die 2 shows 6' are independent: P(both) = (1/6)(1/6) = 1/36. If P(A) = 1/3, P(B) = 1/4, then P(A ∪ B) = 1/3 + 1/4 − 1/12 = 1/2.

right.label: Mutually exclusive events
right.rule: Both CANNOT happen together: A ∩ B = ∅, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Knowing B occurred makes P(A|B) = 0 — which is the OPPOSITE of independence whenever P(A) > 0.
right.example: Single card drawn from a deck: 'card is a heart' and 'card is a spade' are mutually exclusive, so P(heart ∪ spade) = 13/52 + 13/52 = 1/2. But 'heart' and 'king' are INDEPENDENT, not exclusive (king of hearts exists).

left.label: Singular matrix
left.rule: A square matrix A with |A| = 0. It has NO inverse, its rows/columns are linearly dependent, and the system AX = B either has no solution or infinitely many. Adjoint exists but A·adj(A) = 0.
left.example: A = ⎛1 2 3; 2 k 6; 3 6 9⎞ is singular when k = 4 (R₃ = 3R₁). Also ⎛x 2; 8 x⎞ is singular at x = ±4, so det = 0 gives x² = 16.

right.label: Non-singular matrix
right.rule: |A| ≠ 0, so A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A| exists and is unique. Rows/columns are linearly independent; AX = B has a unique solution X = A⁻¹B. Key identities: |A⁻¹| = 1/|A|, |adj A| = |A|^{n−1}, |kA| = kⁿ|A|.
